topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; framework may require adaptation for Australian healthcare systems, funding models, and regulatory environment.
takeaways: Identifies core digital competencies needed in public health roles — use this to audit which skills your team currently lacks and prioritise upskilling in high-impact areas like data literacy and digital tool proficiency.

Scoping review approach means the framework synthesises existing competency models across Europe; check whether the competencies map to your organisation's specific role profiles before rolling out training programs.

European public health focus means frameworks may prioritise different competencies than Australian workplace contexts; localise recommendations to align with your sector's digital maturity and strategic priorities.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears focused on public health faculty development; applicability to other sectors or non-academic settings unclear without full text.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption in public health can be reframed as a development opportunity; structured faculty development programs may be more effective than top-down AI implementation mandates.
Public health educators need targeted upskilling to teach AI literacy credibly; investing in faculty confidence and competence first creates a cascade effect for student AI literacy.

Change management for AI adoption in academic public health requires addressing underlying concerns (job displacement, adequacy of existing knowledge) rather than assuming resistance is simply anti-technology sentiment.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on Generation Z and educational strategies, but geographic scope and specific educational systems examined are not clear from the title and snippet provided. Findings may vary significantly by country and educational context.
takeaways: Identify which AI literacy competencies are most critical for your workforce demographic (e.g., Gen Z employees) rather than assuming uniform skill needs across all age groups.

Design training that moves beyond technical AI knowledge to include broader capabilities like critical thinking and adaptability, which research suggests are essential for sustained employability in AI-driven roles.
Evaluate whether your current onboarding or L&D programs explicitly address the AI skills gap identified in cohort-based analyses, or if they assume baseline knowledge that may not exist.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development would require translation and adaptation.
takeaways: AI competencies should be embedded within a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught in isolation, helping learners understand AI's relationship to other digital tools and skills.

A holistic approach for middle school students suggests starting AI literacy foundations early; apply this principle to adult training by building on foundational digital skills before introducing advanced AI concepts.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited information from snippet alone — appears to address higher education sector broadly, but geographic scope and methodological rigor cannot be assessed from title and snippet provided.
takeaways: Higher education institutions can embed AI competency development through structured curriculum design rather than treating AI literacy as standalone modules.
Identify which AI competencies matter most for your discipline or role — technical skills, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and ethical reasoning may be weighted differently across fields.

articles.title: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to higher vocational education context; geographic scope unclear from snippet. Findings may not generalise to other educational sectors (e.g. universities, secondary schools) or non-academic workplace settings.
takeaways: A validated competency-based ladder approach can structure AI literacy development in stages, potentially applicable to designing progressive learning pathways for employees transitioning from basic AI awareness to advanced capabilities.

The vocational education context suggests practical, skills-focused outcomes — consider adopting similar 'ladder' frameworks when designing AI upskilling programs that map concrete competencies rather than abstract knowledge.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — depends on sample size, sector composition, and geographic scope of surveyed employees. The theoretical framework (Automation–Augmentation Paradox) may apply broadly, but real-world effects likely vary by role, AI literacy, and organisational context.
takeaways: Generative AI can paradoxically both replace and enhance employee knowledge work — managers should explicitly design workflows to ensure AI augments rather than deskills staff, especially in roles where knowledge retention matters.

Monitor knowledge behaviour changes (e.g. over-reliance on AI, reduced learning from problem-solving) when rolling out generative AI tools, as unintended consequences on employee capability development may take time to surface.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings on paternalistic leadership and psychological ownership may have stronger applicability in Asian organisational contexts where this leadership style is more prevalent; generalisability to Western hierarchical structures uncertain without full methodology review.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by involving employees in customising or 'crafting' AI implementations to their specific workflows—this drives genuine collaboration rather than tool compliance.

Under paternalistic leadership styles, employee-AI adoption improves when leaders emphasise care and guidance; ensure your leadership approach balances supportive mentoring with clear AI integration expectations.

Recognise that employees who feel ownership over AI solutions engage more actively in learning and adapting to them—involve teams early in AI tool selection and configuration rather than imposing ready-made systems.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The moderating mechanisms (self-efficacy and transformational leadership) are likely applicable across sectors and geographies, but the strength of effects may vary by industry, AI maturity, and organisational context.
takeaways: Build employee self-efficacy through targeted AI upskilling and mastery experiences — this psychological resource directly buffers against AI-related job insecurity regardless of the pace of AI adoption.

Train managers in transformational leadership practices (inspirational communication, individualised support, intellectual stimulation) to counteract job insecurity during AI implementation — leadership style matters as much as technology itself.
When introducing AI systems, simultaneously address both capability development and leadership culture; neglecting either leaves employees vulnerable to insecurity and disengagement.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — appears to be a theoretical or empirical study, but sample size, geography, and sector scope cannot be assessed from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) in teams to unlock innovation when deploying AI tools — employees with higher PsyCap are more likely to see AI as enabling rather than threatening.

Frame AI as a job resource rather than a replacement threat in your change communication — this cognitive reframing can shift how employees engage with algorithm-driven systems and willingness to experiment.

articles.title: Algorithmic anxiety: AI, work, and the evolving psychological contract in digital discourse - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic anxiety: AI, work, and the evolving psychological contract in digital discourse  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a discourse analysis of digital conversations; sample composition, geography, and industry sectors not clearly specified from title and snippet alone. Findings may reflect vocal online populations rather than broader workforce sentiment.
takeaways: Algorithmic anxiety is shaping how employees perceive the implicit contract between themselves and their employers; managers should monitor and address concerns about AI's role in performance evaluation, job security, and autonomy.

Digital discourse reveals evolving expectations around transparency and fairness in AI deployment; organisations that explicitly communicate how AI tools will be used, what data drives decisions, and how human judgment remains central can reduce anxiety and strengthen trust.

Employee anxiety signals an opportunity to revisit the psychological contract — clarify how AI augments rather than replaces roles, and involve staff in design and rollout decisions to rebuild confidence.

articles.title: Approach or avoidance? A dual-pathway model of job crafting in response to generative AI and its impact on career sustainability - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Approach or avoidance? A dual-pathway model of job crafting in response to generative AI and its impact on career sustainability  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methods — depends on sample composition, size, and sector representation. The dual-pathway model may not apply equally across all job types or organisational contexts.
takeaways: Employees can respond to AI disruption through two distinct pathways: approach-oriented job crafting (expanding AI-related skills and tasks) versus avoidance-oriented crafting (minimising AI exposure). Understanding which pathway your team naturally gravitates toward helps you design targeted upskilling or support interventions.

Career sustainability in an AI-enabled workplace appears linked to how employees proactively reshape their roles. Help staff move beyond passive resistance by creating structured opportunities to experiment with new AI-adjacent responsibilities and reflect on long-term career relevance.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford business school perspective without specified empirical data, sample, or geographic focus. Likely reflects US-centric institutional viewpoint.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI adoption could create behavioural friction points (resistance, skill gaps, role ambiguity) and design change interventions to address these before implementation.

Map AI-driven changes against employee identity and status concerns — people often resist not the technology itself but perceived threats to expertise or career progression, so communication about reskilling pathways and new role opportunities is critical.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to full article, geographic scope and sample characteristics cannot be confirmed. Generalisability depends on whether study includes diverse sectors, organization sizes, and geographic regions.
takeaways: Understanding approach-avoidance dynamics helps predict whether employees will proactively reshape their roles when AI is introduced — use this framework to identify which team members might resist vs. embrace job changes and tailor change management accordingly.

Monitor job crafting behaviors during AI rollouts; employees who avoid adapting their work may experience disengagement or skill obsolescence, so targeted support for those showing avoidance patterns can improve adoption outcomes.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on BCG's client work and consulting experience, likely skewed toward large organisations in developed economies with resources for AI transformation programmes.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology implementation — prioritise identifying skill gaps and designing targeted upskilling pathways before deploying new tools.

Recognise that behaviour change requires addressing mindset and confidence alongside technical training; employees need to see AI as augmenting their role, not replacing it, to drive genuine adoption.

Design change management interventions around psychological safety and early wins — start with high-impact, low-risk use cases where teams can build confidence and demonstrate value before scaling across the organisation.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reflects McKinsey's advisory experience across large organisations, but insights may be most applicable to enterprise-scale companies with significant resources for change management.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling not as a standalone training initiative but as a core organisational change programme with executive sponsorship, clear metrics, and integration into business strategy — this increases adoption and embedding.

Design change interventions that address both skill gaps and mindset shifts, recognising that resistance to AI upskilling often stems from role anxiety and identity threat rather than capability alone.
Establish feedback loops and early-win pilots within teams to build momentum and social proof, rather than rolling out organisation-wide programmes that may overwhelm change capacity.

articles.title: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition, which are not detailed in the snippet. The theoretical framework (conservation of resources theory) is broadly applicable, but geographic scope and sector representation are unclear.
takeaways: Employee attitudes toward AI ('liking of AI') significantly moderate the relationship between AI adoption and outcomes — invest in building positive perceptions of AI tools, not just implementing them technically.

Job crafting and career commitment are key pathways through which AI adoption affects employee wellbeing — design AI integration to enable employees to reshape their roles actively rather than having changes imposed on them.

Use a conservation of resources lens when planning AI rollout: consider how adoption depletes employee resources (cognitive load, autonomy concerns) and design mitigation strategies to maintain engagement and commitment.

articles.title: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone — the full article details are needed to determine sample size, geographic scope, sector coverage, and methodology. DEI interventions vary significantly across countries and regulatory contexts, so geographic applicability should be verified.
takeaways: DEI interventions and diversity-supportive organisational culture can meaningfully moderate the impact of AI on work design — consider auditing your current culture and DEI practices before rolling out AI tools to ensure inclusive implementation.

Algorithmic work design choices (e.g. how AI assigns tasks, sets performance metrics, or provides feedback) interact with your existing DEI efforts; misalignment can amplify bias or exclusion, so involve DEI leads and frontline teams early in AI deployment planning.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Findings likely apply broadly to human memory and personality, though specific generalisability depends on sample composition and methodology not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: Some personalities remember surprising moments better than others—your trait openness or neuroticism might actually shape what sticks in your mind during unexpected events.

The counterintuitive bit: it's not just that surprising things are memorable for everyone; how well you remember them depends on who you are, suggesting personality acts as a filter for what your brain prioritises.

Why it matters: shows that memory isn't a neutral recording device but deeply personal, shaped by your psychological makeup—explaining why two people witnessing the same shocking event often have wildly different recollections.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear without access to full article — depends on size and diversity of wine review sample analyzed, but likely limited to English-language reviews from specific platforms.
takeaways: Wine review language reveals personality traits — what people choose to describe in a glass says something real about how they see the world.
AI can spot patterns in subjective writing that humans might miss, opening quirky new ways to understand personality outside traditional psychometric tests.
Your wine tasting notes might say more about you than you realize — a fun reminder that personality leaks into everyday choices and preferences.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-driven summary of neuroimaging research without visibility of original study design, sample size, or geographic scope. Readers should seek the underlying peer-reviewed publication for methodological details.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies consistently show structural or functional differences in psychopathic individuals, yet these differences don't neatly predict behaviour — a fascinating reminder that brain anatomy alone isn't destiny.

The gap between 'shocking' neurological findings and real-world understanding remains huge: neuroscience can spot differences but struggles to explain why some people with similar brain patterns behave very differently.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — geographic scope and study design not specified. Findings may reflect correlational data from a specific population and require replication.
takeaways: Hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid) has been linked to increased dark personality traits — a counterintuitive connection between a metabolic condition and psychological characteristics.
This finding highlights how physical health conditions can influence personality expression in unexpected ways, blurring the line between biology and behaviour.

The result is surprising because we typically don't think of thyroid function as a driver of narcissism, machiavellianism, or psychopathy — making it a fun reminder that personality is more complex than we assume.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — cross-cultural research suggesting music-personality links are universal rather than culturally specific.
takeaways: Your taste in music might be a surprisingly reliable window into your personality, regardless of where you grow up — suggesting some personality-music links are hardwired rather than learned.

The fact that music preferences align with personality traits across different cultures is counterintuitive given how much musical styles vary globally; it hints that we're responding to something deep about rhythm, harmony, or emotional content rather than just following cultural trends.
This opens a fun thought experiment: if a stranger's playlist can predict whether they're introverted or adventurous, what does that say about how universal human psychology really is?

articles.title: New relationships take a surprising physical toll on older adults - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New relationships take a surprising physical toll on older adults  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on a single study; geographic scope and sample characteristics not evident from snippet. Findings may not generalise across all older adult populations or cultural contexts.
takeaways: Falling in love later in life comes with unexpected physical costs — the stress and adjustment of new relationships can outweigh the emotional benefits for older adults.

Counterintuitive finding: we typically assume romantic relationships improve wellbeing, but new partnerships in older age appear to trigger measurable physical strain, suggesting the body's stress response doesn't discriminate by age.
Highlights that human relationships are physiologically complex — even positive life changes can come with biological costs that vary dramatically depending on life stage.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — appears to be a theoretical or empirical study on psychological capital and AI integration, but geographic scope and sample characteristics are unclear from the title and snippet alone. Findings likely apply across sectors with algorithm-driven work, though validation across diverse organisational contexts would strengthen generalisability.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) as a foundation for psychological safety when introducing AI tools — employees with stronger internal resources are better positioned to view AI as an enabler rather than a threat.

Frame AI as a job resource rather than a replacement threat in internal communication and change management; this reframing can unlock innovation potential and reduce defensive responses to automation.

Invest in developing employees' confidence and resilience before or alongside AI implementation — psychological safety grows when people feel they have the personal resources to adapt and contribute meaningfully alongside AI systems.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings are specific to academic settings with multicultural teams; generalisability to corporate or other organisational contexts unclear. Sample characteristics and size unknown from snippet.
takeaways: AI tools can be designed to prompt leaders toward more inclusive behaviours; consider implementing AI-assisted reminders or decision-support systems that flag potential gender or cultural bias in team interactions and resource allocation.

Algorithmic approaches to inclusive leadership may help standardise fairness practices across teams, but effectiveness likely depends on leader buy-in and integration with broader psychological safety initiatives rather than AI alone.
Monitor outcomes for multicultural teams separately from homogeneous groups — what works to improve inclusion for women or minority team members may differ by cultural context.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings depend on the study's sample size, industry sector, and geographic location, which are not evident from the title and snippet alone. Results may not generalise across all organisational contexts or cultural settings.
takeaways: Leaders must actively foster psychological safety when introducing AI systems; failure to do so creates a pathway to employee depression and reduced wellbeing.

Ethical leadership is a critical moderator in AI adoption — organisations that combine AI implementation with transparent ethical frameworks and leader integrity experience better psychological outcomes than those that do not.

Monitor employee mental health and psychological safety metrics during and after AI adoption rollouts; depression and reduced safety are warning signs that implementation strategy or leadership approach needs adjustment.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG research typically draws on global client work and surveys, but specific sample size, sectors, and geographic distribution are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Create conditions where all employees feel safe to speak up without fear of embarrassment or retaliation — this reduces knowledge hoarding and enables less-heard voices (junior staff, underrepresented groups) to contribute, improving decision-making quality.

Psychological safety is particularly valuable for levelling hierarchical power dynamics; deliberately solicit input from quieter team members and model vulnerability at leadership level to normalise speaking up across organisational levels.

articles.title: The Power of Psychological Safety in Health Care Teams - Yale School of Medicine
articles.snippet: The Power of Psychological Safety in Health Care Teams  Yale School of Medicine
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are grounded in health care settings, which have distinct hierarchies and safety-critical cultures, but may not generalise equally to non-medical organisational contexts. Insights about team dynamics are likely transferable, but implementation specifics may need adaptation for different sectors.
takeaways: Establish explicit norms where team members feel safe voicing concerns and admitting mistakes without fear of punishment or humiliation — particularly important in hierarchical settings where junior staff may hesitate to challenge senior colleagues.

Create structured opportunities (e.g., pre-shift briefings, post-event debriefs) for team members to speak up about potential risks or process improvements, as psychological safety alone is insufficient without formal channels.

Model vulnerability and openness at leadership level — leaders who acknowledge their own limitations and invite dissent from subordinates create environments where psychological safety becomes embedded rather than performative.

articles.title: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty - MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.snippet: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty  MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents conceptual framework relevant to innovation management, but lacks empirical validation or specific organisational context. Principles may apply broadly but are not tested across different sectors or geographies.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that reward admitting uncertainty and challenging assumptions — intellectual honesty requires psychological safety where people feel safe saying 'I don't know' or 'I disagree' without career risk.

When evaluating innovation proposals, actively seek out dissenting views and alternative interpretations rather than consensus — disagreement signals deeper thinking and reduces groupthink that stifles novel solutions.

Model intellectual honesty from leadership by publicly acknowledging what you were wrong about, what you don't understand, and what evidence contradicts your initial views — this sets the cultural tone for the team.
